t: You Can Tell a Lot About a Man by How He Treats Women https://thewaysofagentleman.substack.com/p/you-can-tell-a-lot-about-a-man-by-how-he-treats-women
q: Every woman you meet has a life beyond the few moments you spend with her. She has parents who love her. She has hopes, fears, ambitions, insecurities, and dreams for her future.
One approach treats a woman as a means to satisfy our desires; the other recognizes that how we treat a woman is a reflection of our own character.
If the relationship ends, allow it to end with dignity. Don’t humiliate her afterward by sharing intimate details with your friends.

Pornography encourages a man to separate a woman’s body from her humanity. The person on the screen becomes something to be consumed for gratification, and that mindset probably won’t stay confined to a screen.
Not every desire deserves to be satisfied. There are a lot of things a man might want that wisdom tells him to resist.
Self-control isn’t a weakness; it’s one of the clearest demonstrations of strength. Any man can surrender to his appetites, but it takes discipline to govern them.
It’s easy to behave respectfully when a woman is standing right in front of you. The bigger test comes when she isn’t standing there.
A man’s character isn’t revealed by what he can get away with. It’s revealed by what he refuses to do even when he could.
x: Treating a woman as a person with parents, hopes and a future, never as a means to pleasure, should change how a man approaches dating, including how he ends a relationship.
The test of a man's character is how he treats a woman when his desires and his honor pull in different directions, not how well he performs courtesies in public.
Respect is tested in private: how a man speaks about women among other men, and whether he joins crude talk or shares intimate details to impress friends.

t: The Growing Threat to Executive and Expert Careers
q: Senior experts face a different version of the same problem. The knowledge and experience that established their value are becoming easier to access, reproduce and challenge.
Even sound judgements are more vulnerable to scrutiny. Anyone with an AI assistant can produce a plausible alternative, whether or not they understand the underlying problem.

The answer is not simply to work harder, acquire another qualification or learn a few new AI tools. It requires a different approach to understanding the world, making decisions and exercising influence.
The danger is no longer simply not knowing enough. It is not knowing what you need to know.

Waiting for certainty can become as dangerous as acting prematurely. The challenge is to distinguish reliable evidence from plausible speculation, recognise competing explanations and understand the implications of different choices.

AI can contribute enormously to this process. It can challenge assumptions, examine alternatives and expose weaknesses in an argument. But it can also generate convincing errors and misleading confidence.

More argument, more evidence or greater formal authority may not resolve the problem. You need to understand how the system actually operates, anticipate its responses and create conditions in which progress becomes possible.
Not executives who surrender their judgement to AI, but those who use it intelligently while retaining responsibility for their decisions.

q: But students are then going to “tick and fix”. Will correcting mistakes in green pen make any difference? The answer is no.
These take time, and do nothing to put the information in long term memory. It may help short term memory - but this will be up to the student.

The teacher says, out loud, the thought that is troubling them. This offloads the thought, so they can stop worrying about it. They critique their own teaching live, and then immediately ignore that critique. The opportunity to improve is lost.
Compliance is the goal of the routine, not learning. Her instincts know this. But she has to suppress them.
Then she asks students to chant it back to her. That is performance, it is not recall. It is compliance, but not learning.
Why correct this way? Because it is from memory, another retrieval.
You don’t want to see students’ corrections. You want to see what they still don’t know.
Only one transition. No mini white board. No green pens high in the sky. No corrections at the visualiser. No checking for understanding. No chanting. No interruptions!
x: The author argues pen colour has no effect on how memorable a correction is.
Copying corrections consumes time without securing long-term memory.
Teachers who voice doubts and then ignore them stop improving.
The routine rewards compliance, which differs from learning.
Chanting an answer back is performance and not recall.
Making corrections from memory turns them into more retrieval practice.
Assessment should reveal gaps, not display tidy corrected work.
A pen-free question sequence reduces teacher effort and increases learning.

q: It is not that we choose one thing over another, rather that we place one thing ahead of the other. Foreground and background. Our differences often come down to composition.
First, there is surrogation, where we mistake the metric for the goal, leading to a distortion of behaviour. The classic educational example of this is ‘teaching to the test’.
Belonging is a desirable outcome of a well-run school and is a achieved by foregrounding high educational standards.

If oracy becomes the thing - the foreground in our instructional composition - strange things start to happen. We reify a rhetorical abstraction, look for ways to assess it, create metrics to measure it, then seek to improve it as if it is a thing quite separate from what the pupil knows.

The fundamental principle is that effective teaching should be ‘good for the many, vital for the few’. In other words, it is those who find learning hardest, or who are at greatest disadvantage, who should benefit most from instruction.
The schools I have known where relationships between adults and children are the most positive are the ones who do not foreground relationships.
Knowledge and skills are not a pendulum. You can’t think of this debate as one where the pendulum tipped too far towards skills, but now you want to avoid it tipping too far towards knowledge.
It is not whether a new policy or strategy is a good thing but whether it is a better thing than what it replaces and distracts us from.
x: Evans reframes many education disputes as disagreements about composition, not binary choice.
Confusing a metric with the goal distorts behaviour, as in teaching to the test.
Belonging results from high standards and good teaching rather than being a standalone aim.
Making oracy the focus detaches it from knowledge and invites metrics that distort teaching.
Explicit instruction is justified on social justice grounds because it helps the least advantaged most.
Strong cultural norms, not a relational focus, produce the calm in which relationships flourish.
Knowledge is the pathway to skill, so the two should not be framed as competing poles.
Every new initiative must be judged by what it displaces, because school resources are finite.

t: Screen Time and AI Need Different Questions
q: The screen-time conversation asks how much time children spend with media, what they encounter, and what that time replaces. The AI conversation also asks who is doing the thinking, whether information is accurate, whose work is being presented, and what happens to student data.

When we collapse those questions into one argument about devices, we make it harder to address either well. A limit on screen minutes cannot tell us whether a student understands an AI-assisted answer.

A school should be able to explain why a digital activity deserves students’ time. Calling something educational does not automatically make it worthwhile. Nor does an engaging app earn unlimited access to the school day.

Consider a teacher using AI to generate possible discussion questions, then checking and adapting them before a device-free seminar. The teacher has used AI. Students have not added a minute of screen exposure.

A 2025 high-school mathematics experiment makes the distinction concrete. Students using an open-ended AI tool performed better during assisted practice but worse on a later unassisted assessment than students without it.
Better-looking work and stronger understanding are different outcomes. We need to check both.
What does it replace? A ten-minute activity may be reasonable on its own and still add to a day already crowded with screens.
We owe families a clearer explanation than being for or against screens. We owe students opportunities to learn with useful tools and opportunities to learn without them.
x: Screen time concerns exposure, sleep, movement and what the time replaces, while AI raises separate questions about who is doing the thinking, accuracy, authorship and student data.

Review every activity from both directions, its effect on time and attention and its effect on thinking, responsibility and safety, because the concerns can coexist in one lesson.
Screen time and AI are different policy questions: one is about exposure and displacement, the other about who does the thinking, accuracy, authorship and privacy.

q: Our advantage is that Comparative Judgement creates a fine grained measurement scale for oracy.

Our limitation, however, is that oracy is hard to assess, so unlike most of our other posts the samples in our study are small, which restricts the forms of analysis we can perform and limits our findings.
The correlation was 0.43, higher than the 0.34 reported in the meta-analysis1.
What is really striking is how improvement slows with age. Yes, these are small samples, but we see exactly the same in our writing composition data.

In both studies pupils with pupil premium status2 scored lower on average than the rest of the cohort. The gap is about 0.4 of a standard deviation3, broadly comparable with national English assessments at KS2.
Most of them mentioned features that are highly rated in written communication – including sentence structure.

Our findings suggest that oracy is not necessarily an area of hidden strength for pupils who struggle with writing: pupils encounter many of the same challenges in spoken and written expression, while teachers value similar features in each.
Finally, if we believe that oracy is a priority, then our data suggests it is the younger pupils we should focus on. Oracy, just like writing, gets harder to improve as pupils get older.
x: Comparative Judgement lets the studies measure oracy on a finer scale than the three national grades.
The authors admit small samples limit what the analysis can establish.
Oracy and writing correlate more strongly here than in the published meta-analysis.
Oracy progress slows with age just as writing progress does.
Disadvantaged pupils trail in oracy by a margin similar to writing.
Teachers reward written-style features such as sentence structure when judging speech.
Struggling writers are not hidden oracy stars, since both skills draw on shared challenges.
If oracy is prioritised, younger pupils offer the better return.

t: Nature Doesn’t Know It’s Called Biology
q: Science, however, sat somewhere in the background. I admired people who knew it well, but I had convinced myself that it belonged to someone else.
We categorise ourselves into subjects we enjoy and subjects we don’t, rarely stopping to question whether those categories actually exist anywhere outside school.
The concept of Consilience argues that reality itself has never been divided. Only our study of it has.

Science is not merely a way of asking questions; it is humanity’s collective memory of the answers we have discovered so far. Schools have the responsibility of ensuring every child inherits that memory before asking them to extend it.
Philosophies often begin with ideals about how learning ought to occur. Science begins by asking what actually happens when human beings learn.

A child is simultaneously a biological organism, a chemical system, a physical body and a social being. Therefore, to understand our students, we need to understand something about all of those things.
Not because every child will become a scientist, but because every child is already living inside the systems science seeks to explain.
x: The author admits to the same limiting self-labelling that teachers criticise in students.
School subject categories are human constructs that do not exist in nature itself.
Disciplines are lenses on one reality, so their divisions are artefacts of study.
Science is accumulated knowledge that schools must hand on before asking pupils to extend it.
Evidence-based science differs from philosophy in starting from observed learning rather than ideals.
Understanding pupils fully requires knowledge across biology, chemistry, physics and the social sciences.
The case for central science is universal exposure, not producing future scientists.

t: Keeping Up with AI When the Classroom Is the Frontier
q: AI may not be inevitable, but for many, it has already happened, and that’s caused a lot of problems.
In education, if you take the time to develop something and integrate it, you don’t expect it to disappear or radically change months later!

We’re going to need to develop a social contract around AI and its place in our world. In order to do that, we have to figure out a way to stay informed about AI and talk to one another about it, not past each other.
Agents operate in autonomous loops, using tools to look up information, code interactives, and use machine reasoning to check and recheck responses.

This matters because your engagement with AI often informs your stance on it, and if your main interaction with AI is through freemium models, or not at all, then you likely struggle to understand what the actual capabilities are of more advanced agentic systems currently on the market.
At its core is a design problem. Developers have optimized interfaces for agentic tasks, where human review and interaction is often considered ancillary, when it should be centered on that dynamic.
If someone read a disclosure note and came up to you and asked how you used AI, would you be able to articulate what your role was vs. an agent?
I also don’t believe that curiosity about AI needs to equal fluency with an AI tool or product

Having on-ramps and off-ramps that allow people to choose their comfort level with AI will continue to be a meaningful design decision for me, because choice should matter and not always default to the newest shiny thing as the norm.

t: Inclusive For Whom, and at What Cost?
q: A sentence everyone endorses cannot effectively guide everyday workplace practice, and it’s even less useful when things go badly wrong.
Attitude matters, of course, but we should consider it a starting condition, not a method.
Design problems have constraints, trade-offs and costs. They improve through iteration and evidence, not through goodwill.
An organisation that pretends there are no trade-offs will still make them. It will just make them invisibly, and usually in favour of whoever happens to fit the default.
In short, diversity can increase the range of perspectives available to a team. But it can also increase the work required to integrate them.
Belonging without uniqueness is assimilation. Uniqueness without belonging often results in being tolerated at the margins. Only the two together amount to inclusion.
Celebrating cognitive differences is easy enough. Designing workplaces intentionally and meaningfully around cognitive differences is much harder
A realist asks for the cost to be named, and then asks who is carrying it.
An organisation that can say “Here is what we are trading off, and why” is closer to inclusion than one that can only say “Everyone is welcome”.
x: His conclusion is that no workplace is universally inclusive, and the useful question is inclusive for whom, under what conditions and at what cost, with the cost named and its bearer identified.
Inclusion is a design problem, not common sense: attitude is a starting condition, and real decisions about meetings, assignments, evaluation and space always involve trade-offs.

q: Too many organizations still treat cybersecurity as something only the IT department handles. That framing is convenient but dead wrong.

People trust leaders with their livelihoods, their personal information, and their reputations. Protecting that trust cannot be handed off entirely to specialists, any more than integrity can be relegated to the legal department.
Team members pay closer attention to what leaders do than to what policy says.
The team member who clicks a bad link and says so within minutes is an asset, not a problem child. The one who hides it for fear of blame can turn an incident into a serious breach.
Security is, and always has been, a set of choices about risk, and those choices belong at the leadership table, not solely with IT.
They require two approvals for large payments, confirm any change in account details through a second channel, and ensure access ends when a role ends.
Attackers count on busy people who trust too quickly and leaders who assume someone else is watching.
x: The piece argues that cybersecurity is a leadership responsibility, not something to hand off to the IT department.
The author frames security as stewardship, since people trust leaders with their livelihoods, personal information and reputations.
The piece argues that cybersecurity is a leadership responsibility, not something to hand off to the IT department.
Making it safe to report a clicked bad link within minutes turns a possible breach into a contained incident; blame drives people to hide mistakes.
What data to hold, for how long, who can access it and which vendors to trust are risk decisions that belong to leaders, not only to IT.
Resilient processes beat heroic individuals: two approvals on large payments, second-channel confirmation of banking changes, and access that ends when a role ends.
Because many attacks exploit human trust rather than code, every leader who directs people or controls a budget is already part of the security perimeter.
